title: Preaching the Word
summary: How to prepare and deliver faithful, clear and applied sermons: the theology of preaching, studying a passage, building an expository sermon, and preaching with power and integrity.
description: "Preach the word" (2 Timothy 4:2). This course is for pastors, evangelists and lay preachers who want to handle God's Word faithfully. It covers why we preach, the preacher's life, studying a passage in context, finding the main idea, structuring an expository sermon, illustrating and applying, delivering with clarity and conviction, and avoiding common errors in preaching.
objectives: Explain the biblical theology and purpose of preaching
Study a passage carefully to find its meaning
Build an expository sermon from the main idea of a text
Deliver sermons clearly and with integrity
outcomes: Explain why expository preaching serves the church
Move from text to main idea to sermon outline
Write a sermon introduction and conclusion
Apply a passage to real lives in your context
Evaluate sermons for faithfulness and clarity

modules.title: Why We Preach
modules.intro: Preaching is God's chosen means to save and build His people. This week we study its theology and the preacher's life.

lessons.title: God speaks through preaching
lessons.body:
"For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe" (1 Corinthians 1:21). "How shall they hear without a preacher?" (Romans 10:14).

When the Word is faithfully preached, God speaks: the Thessalonians received Paul's preaching "not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe" (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

This is why Paul charged Timothy solemnly, "before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ... Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Timothy 4:1-2).

lessons.title: Expository preaching
lessons.body:
**Expository preaching** explains and applies the meaning of a Bible passage, so that the main point of the text becomes the main point of the sermon. Ezra's helpers "read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:8).

Benefits: it lets God set the agenda; it teaches people how to read the Bible; it covers "all the counsel of God" (Acts 20:27), including hard texts; and it protects the preacher from repeating favourite themes.

**Topical** sermons can also be faithful when each point is drawn properly from Scripture in context. The danger is using texts as pegs for the preacher's own ideas.

lessons.title: The preacher's life
lessons.body:
"Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee" (1 Timothy 4:16).

The preacher must:

- Be a **Christian** who lives what he preaches (1 Corinthians 9:27).
- Be a man or woman of **the Word**, studying diligently (2 Timothy 2:15).
- Be a person of **prayer**: the apostles gave themselves "to prayer, and to the ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4).
- Depend on the **Spirit**: "my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power" (1 Corinthians 2:4).
- Be **humble**: we are clay pots carrying treasure (2 Corinthians 4:7).

modules.title: Studying the Passage
modules.intro: Faithful sermons begin with careful study. This week we move from reading to understanding a passage.

lessons.title: Choose and pray over the text
lessons.body:
Choose a passage that is a complete unit of thought: a paragraph, a story or a psalm. Preaching through a book of the Bible over several weeks helps the church grasp context and avoids 'hobby horses'.

Begin with prayer: "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" (Psalm 119:18).

Read the passage many times, in more than one translation if possible, and read the whole book or chapter around it. Start study early in the week, not on Saturday night. "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2:15).

lessons.title: Observe, interpret, apply
lessons.body:
Use the three steps of Bible study:

1. **Observe**: What does it say? Note who, what, where, when, key words, repeated words, commands, contrasts and connectives (therefore, but, because).
2. **Interpret**: What did it mean to the first hearers? Consider the literary type (story, poem, letter, prophecy), historical background, the flow of the book, and other Scripture ("comparing spiritual things with spiritual", 1 Corinthians 2:13). Check good commentaries after your own study.
3. **Apply**: What does it mean for us now? What truth about God, warning, promise, example or command is here?

Ezra "prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:10): study, obey, then teach.

lessons.title: Christ in all the Scriptures
lessons.body:
Jesus taught that the Scriptures "testify of me" (John 5:39). On the Emmaus road, "beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27).

A Christian sermon on any text should ask how the passage relates to Christ: through prophecy, through types and patterns (like the Passover lamb), through the need it reveals that only Christ meets, or through the character of God fulfilled in Christ.

This guards against moralism, which preaches only "Be like David" without showing David's greater Son. Paul "determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Corinthians 2:2).

modules.title: Building the Sermon
modules.intro: A sermon needs a clear main idea and structure. This week we move from study to outline, illustration and application.

lessons.title: The main idea
lessons.body:
Every good sermon has one **main idea**, the big point of the text, stated in one clear sentence.

First find the passage's **subject** (what is it talking about?) and **complement** (what is it saying about that?). For example, Psalm 23: subject, the LORD as shepherd; complement, He provides, guides and protects His people in every season. Main idea: "Because the LORD is my shepherd, I lack nothing I truly need, in life or death."

Then ask the **purpose**: what should hearers believe, feel or do as a result? A sermon that cannot be summarised in a sentence is probably unclear.

lessons.title: Outline, introduction and conclusion
lessons.body:
Build the **outline** from the text's own structure. Each main point should explain part of the main idea and come from the passage. Use clear, parallel headings; two to four points are usually enough.

The **introduction** gets attention, raises the need the text answers, and introduces the passage. Keep it short.

The **conclusion** restates the main idea, applies it, and calls for a response: to repent, believe, obey, give thanks. Peter's sermon ended with a clear call: "Repent, and be baptized" (Acts 2:38).

Keep to time. Thirty to forty minutes of clear preaching is better than ninety minutes of repetition.

lessons.title: Illustration and application
lessons.body:
**Illustrations** are like windows that let light into the sermon. Jesus used farming, fishing, money, weddings and family life. Use illustrations from everyday Nigerian life, Scripture, history and nature. Make sure they are true, appropriate and serve the point, not just entertain. Avoid sharing others' secrets or embarrassing your family.

**Application** answers "So what?" Be specific: speak to different groups (young people, parents, workers, leaders), to the heart and to actions. Apply first to yourself.

Nathan's parable led to the piercing application, "Thou art the man" (2 Samuel 12:7). Good application is direct, but loving.

modules.title: Delivering the Message
modules.intro: Good preparation needs faithful delivery. This week we study delivery, common errors and growing as a preacher.

lessons.title: Clear and passionate delivery
lessons.body:
Delivery serves the message:

- **Clarity**: speak plainly, at a pace people can follow; explain unfamiliar words.
- **Voice**: vary pace, volume and pitch; pause for emphasis. Shouting is not the same as power.
- **Eye contact and posture**: speak to people, not to your notes.
- **Notes**: use a brief outline rather than reading a full script, but know your material well.
- **Language**: use the language your hearers understand best; work well with interpreters by using short sentences.
- **Passion**: believe what you preach. Paul preached "with many tears" (Acts 20:31).

"Let all things be done unto edifying" (1 Corinthians 14:26).

lessons.title: Common errors
lessons.body:
Avoid:

- **Eisegesis**: reading your own ideas into a text instead of drawing out its meaning.
- **Proof-texting**: using a verse out of context, such as claiming Jeremiah 29:11 as a promise of wealth.
- **Allegorising**: inventing hidden meanings for every detail.
- **Manipulation**: using emotion, guilt or pressure, especially for money (2 Corinthians 2:17; 4:2).
- **Self-promotion**: making yourself the hero of every story (2 Corinthians 4:5).
- **Plagiarism**: preaching another's sermon as your own without credit.
- **Neglecting the gospel**: sermons with no Christ and no grace.

"We have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty... nor handling the word of God deceitfully" (2 Corinthians 4:2).

lessons.title: Growing as a preacher
lessons.body:
Every preacher can grow:

- **Ask for feedback** from trusted, honest listeners: Was the main idea clear? Was it faithful to the text? Was it applied?
- **Listen to good preachers** and learn from their approach.
- **Read widely**: theology, commentaries, biographies and the culture.
- **Keep a sermon file** of ideas, illustrations and passages to preach.
- **Rest and refuel**: "Come ye yourselves apart... and rest a while" (Mark 6:31).

Faithfulness, not fame, is the measure. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6). "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" is the reward to seek (Matthew 25:21).

assignments.title: A sermon manuscript
assignments.prompt: Choose a passage of 5-15 verses. Submit your study notes (observations and interpretation), the main idea in one sentence, a full outline, introduction, illustrations, application and conclusion. Show how the passage points to Christ.

assignments.title: Sermon evaluation
assignments.prompt: Listen to two sermons (in your church or recorded). Evaluate each for faithfulness to the text, clarity of main idea, Christ-centredness, application and delivery, using the principles of this course. Be fair and charitable.
